summary: Catalogs middleboxes, meaning devices between hosts that do more than normal IP routing, such as NATs and firewalls. It cites related IETF work and identifies issues they raise. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A middlebox is an intermediary on a network path that does more than normal IP routing. RFC 3234 sorts examples into categories and explains how they can affect connectivity, failure recovery, security, and application design.

questions: how do middleboxes break the end to end principle
how do middleboxes affect network protocols
what are the eight middlebox facets
subtitle: A taxonomy of network intermediaries that do more than forward IP packets.

tldr.problem: More devices in the network path modify, redirect, or manage traffic, which can affect protocols designed to communicate directly between end systems.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines middleboxes, describes 22 types, classifies them along eight facets, and discusses their effects on architecture, failures, and security.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3234 is an Informational and explicitly non-definitive survey. It recommends that future application protocols account for middleboxes and include clear failure handling.

today: RFC 3234 is an Informational memo published in February 2002. The RFC describes its catalogue and conclusions as preliminary and explicitly says it is not definitive.

sections.title: What Counts as a Middlebox
sections.content:
A middlebox is an intermediary device that performs functions beyond the normal functions of an IP router on the path between a source and destination. It may be a separate device or a function inside another device. Standard IP route selection and forwarding are not middlebox functions under this definition.

The memo relates middleboxes to the Internet's hourglass model and end-to-end principle. Middleboxes can add hidden dependencies and failure modes, require configuration beyond the two end systems, and make failures harder to diagnose. The RFC says its catalogue is not definitive and that some classifications are subjective.
sections.plainLanguage: A middlebox is a device or software function on the path that does more than choose where to forward an IP packet. It can change how traffic reaches its destination and add another point that needs configuration or may fail.

sections.title: Eight Ways to Classify a Middlebox
sections.content:
The RFC uses eight facets rather than arranging middleboxes in one hierarchy. The facets ask which protocol layer the device acts on; whether its role is explicit or implicit; whether one or several boxes can be involved; and whether it sits in-line or calls out to another box.

The other facets ask whether the function is required or only an optimization, whether the box routes or processes traffic, whether it keeps soft or hard state, and whether failure leads to failover or session restart. The memo deliberately does not classify middleboxes as good or bad.
sections.plainLanguage: The same eight questions help compare very different devices. They describe what the device does, where it sits, and what happens if it loses state or fails.

sections.title: Examples in the Catalogue
sections.content:
The catalogue covers 22 types, including network address translators, tunnels, firewalls, transport relays, performance-enhancing proxies, load balancers, application gateways, caches, modified DNS servers, content distribution boxes, and anonymisers. The entries explain each type's role and give its approximate classification across the facets.

The memo describes specific compatibility and integrity concerns. For example, a transport relay that ends one TCP connection and starts another can mean the original TCP checksum no longer covers the data end to end. Tunnels can reduce the available MTU and affect diagnostic ICMP messages. The memo also excludes some devices, including ordinary wiretaps that do not affect traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples range from address translators and firewalls to caches and content distribution systems. Each can affect traffic differently, so the memo describes its role and the problems it may cause.

sections.title: What the Catalogue Suggests
sections.content:
Across the 22 classes, the memo counts 17 as application-layer or multi-layer, 21 as in-line, 16 as using hard state, and 21 as requiring a session restart after failure. These are approximate classifications in a catalogue that the authors say is neither complete nor definitive.

The memo concludes that middleboxes do not make the end-to-end principle useless, but application protocols should be designed with likely middleboxes in mind. It recommends clear failure handling and explicit ways to insert middleboxes. It describes soft state, rapid failover to a spare, and rapid restart by the communicating ends as possible approaches to failures.
sections.plainLanguage: The catalogue suggests that many middleboxes sit directly in the traffic path and keep state needed by a session. The RFC advises protocol designers to expect intermediaries and decide how sessions should recover if one fails.

sections.title: Security and Trust Across the Path
sections.content:
Security risks differ by middlebox type, but every additional device in a path adds another point of attack. Middleboxes can reduce or prevent end-to-end encryption and complicate trust relationships and key distribution. Their management and configuration mechanisms also need protection.

The memo says content caches and distribution mechanisms raise access-control questions for material subject to copyright or other rights. It calls for security analysis specific to each middlebox design rather than offering one security rule for all types.
sections.plainLanguage: Every intermediary adds a system that must be trusted and secured. Some also prevent end-to-end encryption, so each design needs its own security analysis.

items.title: Protocol layer
items.text: IP, transport, upper layers, or a mix.

items.title: Explicit or implicit
items.text: Designed into the protocol or added around it.

items.title: Single-hop or multi-hop
items.text: One box or several boxes in the path.

items.title: In-line or call-out
items.text: On the data path or using an ancillary box.

items.title: Functional or optimizing
items.text: Needed for the session or only improving it.

items.title: Soft or hard state
items.text: Whether a session continues if state is lost.

items.title: Failover or restart
items.text: Whether a failed session moves to a spare or restarts.
